New Mexico Hot Springs Road Trip: 18 Open Soaks, 3 Legs By Alex Duplechain · Facts last reviewed October 31, 2026New Mexico is the free spirit of the directory. Of its 18 open springs, seven allow clothing-optional soaking — 39%. Washington leads at 44%, and New Mexico is second. Next are California (25%), Oregon (21%), Arkansas (20%), and Colorado (16%). The state also runs a genuine split personality: primitive canyon soaks in the Jemez mountains on one end, and a full spa town built on a river in Truth or Consequences on the other. You don't come here for resort luxury — 8 of the 18 are resorts or spas. You come for the range.Three legs cover it the way you'd actually drive it: the Jemez corridor from Albuquerque, the Taos–Ojo Caliente loop in the north, and the Truth or Consequences arc down the Rio Grande. Plan on six to eight days for all three.The numbers: why New Mexico is the free-spirit state20 springs mapped, 18 open. Skip two: the listing literally named Hot Springs in the town of Hot Springs is closed and has zero reviews — it's the directory's worst name trap, don't chase it. Hacienda del Camino Real & Hot Springs in Radium Springs is temporarily closed; at 4.8 from 68 reviews it was the highest-rated spring in the state, so check its status before you drive there.7 of 18 open springs are clothing-optional — second to Washington's 44% share. Faywood Hot Springs, Manby Hot Springs, Black Rock Hot Springs, and San Antonio Hot Springs (by custom) run suits-optional around the clock; the Ojo Caliente Round Barn and Riverbend Hot Springs go clothing-optional after dark. Read our clothing-optional etiquette guide before you go — and note that everywhere else in New Mexico, suits are the default.9 free, 2 mid-priced, 6 in the higher price band. The free springs are real soaks, not consolation prizes — including Montezuma Hot Springs on a paved road.8 resort/spa, 9 primitive/backcountry. The state sits almost evenly split — you'll alternate between built pools and canyon rocks within the same day.5 open springs have campgrounds on site — Faywood, the Round Barn, Riverbend, Jordan, and Gila Hot Springs Campground — so a soak-by-day, camp-by-night itinerary works on the northern loop and the southern leg.The crowd has spoken. Riverbend Hot Springs (4.8 from 4,641 reviews) is the most-reviewed spring in New Mexico and one of the most-reviewed in the entire directory. Hoosier Hot Springs & Inn (4.9 from 197) is the highest-rated spring in the state. When a small inn beats a resort that outdraws it 20-to-1 on reviews, both are worth your time.Truth or Consequences holds four commercial soaks in one town — Riverbend, Blackstone, Hoosier, and Fire Water — the densest paid cluster in New Mexico. The Jemez Mountains hold the densest free cluster, with three free or cheap canyon springs within a few miles.Leg 1: The Jemez corridor — canyon water near AlbuquerqueStart from Albuquerque and run north into the Jemez Mountains, where the volcanic caldera feeds a string of springs along the canyon road. Base yourself in Jemez Springs, which holds three springs within minutes of each other. Spence Hot Springs (free, 4.1 from 525, short walk) is the workhorse — a primitive day-use soak on the Santa Fe National Forest, with no fee and no restrooms, easy access, and a steady crowd, the spring most people mean when they say "Jemez". Jemez Hot Springs ($$, 4.6 from 920, clothing required, paved road) is the better-rated, more built-out option — and notably one of the few New Mexico springs where the policy is explicitly suits-on, so the etiquette is unambiguous. San Antonio Hot Springs (free, clothing-optional by custom, 4.4 from 18) is the quiet third — but not a short walk: the last stretch is a steep, exposed 0.7-mile hike-in, the Forest Service road to it closes seasonally, and the reviews are thin, so treat it as a detour, not a destination.The leg's hike is McCauley Spring (free, 4.6 from 29), a two-mile hike from the Battleship Rock trailhead, by the Forest Service's count — the rating-per-review is excellent but the sample is small and the walk is real. This is the trip's first filter: if the hike sounds like the point, New Mexico is your state. If it sounds like a chore, the T-or-C leg will suit you better.Leg 2: Taos and Ojo Caliente — the northern loopHead north to Ojo Caliente, where the two resort entries of the leg sit minutes apart. Ojo Caliente Mineral Springs Resort & Spa ($$$, 4.5 from 4,198) is the northern anchor and the second-most-reviewed spring in the state — the one big-name destination property in New Mexico. (It's a drive-up: the operator's directions run north from Santa Fe on US-285 for 50 miles, then 0.4 miles on NM-414 to the resort.) The Ojo Caliente Hot Springs Round Barn ($$$, 4.6 from 40, clothing-optional after dark, campground on site) is the smaller, stranger sibling — a genuinely unusual soak, and the campground makes it a natural overnight.East of Ojo, the two free northern soaks reward the driver who keeps going. Montezuma Hot Springs (free, 4.6 from 441, paved road) is the best free value in the north — easy to reach and the rating holds across 441 reviews. Ponce de Leon Springs (free, 4.3 from 17, short walk) is the quieter northern stop; thin reviews, but the access is easy.Then Taos County's clothing-optional pair, both on the primitive end. Manby Hot Springs (free, clothing-optional, 4.1 from 106, hike-in 2 miles one way) and Black Rock Hot Springs (free, clothing-optional, 4.2 from 98, short walk) are the trip's wildest water — name-collision warning: Nevada has a different Black Rock Hot Springs; ours is the Taos County one. Manby takes a real hike, while Black Rock is a short walk: independent trip reports put it about 0.3 mile from the parking area near the John Dunn Bridge (BLM publishes no mileage). Both are suits-optional by policy, not by rumor. Read the etiquette guide first.Leg 3: Truth or Consequences and the southwest — the spa townDrive south down the Rio Grande to the trip's anchor town. Truth or Consequences — the only town in our directory with four commercial soaks inside its limits — and you can hit all four in a day. Riverbend Hot Springs ($$$, 4.8 from 4,641, clothing-optional after dark, campground on site, paved road) is the state's most-reviewed spring and the town's headline — soak in the evening when the pools go suits-optional. Hoosier Hot Springs & Inn ($$$, 4.9 from 197) is the highest-rated spring in New Mexico — small, and the inn stay is the draw. Blackstone Hotsprings ($$$, 4.6 from 816, adult retreat with private rooms) and Fire Water Lodge Hot Springs Spa ($$$, 4.6 from 407) round out the town — both paved-road easy.From T-or-C, the southwest gives you the trip's two outliers. Faywood Hot Springs (paid, clothing-optional, campground on site, paved road) is the full-experience outlier — the one place in the state where you get resort infrastructure, a campground, and an explicit clothing-optional policy all at once. Jordan Hot Springs (free, hike-in, campground on site) near Magdalena is the remote one — the most backcountry spring in the state. Closer to the road, Lightfeather Hot Spring (free, hike-in) sits on the Middle Fork of the Gila about 3/4 mile from the Gila Visitor Center by the Park Service's count, with two river crossings on the way; the source pulses out at about 130°F, so soak in the rock pools in the river, not at the source. Before you drive to Radium Springs, recheck Hacienda del Camino Real — temporarily closed.The 9-free strategyNew Mexico's 9 free springs beat most states' paid lists. The north gives you Montezuma (4.6/441, paved) as the easy anchor, Ponce de Leon (4.3/17) as the quiet add-on, McCauley (4.6/29) as the hike-in reward, and the Taos pair — Manby (4.1/106) and Black Rock (4.2/98), both clothing-optional — as the wild finish. Spence and San Antonio (4.4/18) fill the Jemez leg, and Jordan (3.9/26, campground on site) anchors the remote southwest, with Lightfeather as the short walk from the Gila Visitor Center. Our free hot springs guide covers the national picture; in New Mexico the free set includes a 4.6-rated paved-road soak, which is better than most states manage at any price.Where the money goesSpend at the three big names. Riverbend is the riverside resort on the Rio Grande in T-or-C. Ojo Caliente is the northern destination resort. Hoosier is the splurge — a small inn where the stay is part of the soak. The value play is Faywood — resort water, an explicit clothing-optional policy, and an on-site campground, and the visit is paid.Practical notesThe name trap: the directory contains a listing literally named "Hot Springs" in a town called Hot Springs — it's closed, has zero reviews, and isn't going anywhere. The real soaks are in Truth or Consequences (four), Jemez Springs (three), Taos County (two), and Ojo Caliente (two). Don't chase the name.Clothing policy matters here more than anywhere else. Seven of the 18 open springs run clothing-optional at least part of the day — but that means 11 don't. The Round Barn, Riverbend and Gila Hot Springs Campground are suits-required by day and optional after dark; everywhere else, the policy is what it says on the page. When in doubt, the etiquette guide is the document of record.Verify before you drive. Hacienda del Camino Real is temporarily closed and worth rechecking. Montezuma and Ponce de Leon are paved-road easy.Winter: New Mexico is in our winter-soaking set — see the winter hot springs guide. The Jemez and Taos legs are mountain winter; T-or-C stays mild.Campgrounds: 5 open springs have campgrounds on site — Faywood, the Round Barn, Riverbend, Jordan, and Gila Hot Springs Campground. The budget trip is real: free soaks in the Jemez and Taos, campgrounds in the south, and resort money only at Riverbend and Ojo.Ready to pick one?Answer three questions and we'll rank the springs that fit how you actually want to soak.Open the matcher →
